solution:
A point on the X-axis has \(y\) co-ordinate 0, and it lies to the RIGHT of the origin when its \(x\) co-ordinate is positive.

\((-2, 0)\) is on the X-axis but has \(x = -2 < 0\), so it lies to the left.

\((0, 2)\) is on the Y-axis, not the X-axis.

\((2, 3)\) has \(y = 3 \ne 0\), so it is not on the X-axis at all.

\((2, 0)\) has \(y = 0\) and \(x = 2 > 0\).

\(\therefore\) the required point is \((2, 0)\).

solution:
A segment parallel to the Y-axis joins two points whose \(x\) co-ordinates are equal (only the \(y\) co-ordinate changes as you move up or down).

Point A is \((1, 3)\), so the \(x\) co-ordinate of B must also be 1.

Of the four alternatives only \((1, -3)\) has \(x = 1\); \((3, 1)\) and \((3, 0)\) have \(x = 3\) and \((5, 3)\) has \(x = 5\).

\(\therefore\) the co-ordinates of B can be \((1, -3)\).

The chapter's own rule: "seg PQ is parallel to Y-axis \(\therefore\) \(x\) co-ordinates of points P and Q are equal".

solution:
The chapter defines the slope of a line making an angle \(\theta\) with the positive direction of the X-axis as \(m = \tan\theta\).

\(m = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)

\(\therefore\) the slope of the line is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

(\(\dfrac{1}{2}\) is \(\sin 30^\circ\), \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is \(\cos 30^\circ\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) is \(\tan 60^\circ\), all three are distractors, not the tan ratio of \(30^\circ\).)

solution:
The chapter's "Remember this!" box gives \(d(O, P) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) for a point P\((x, y)\) and the origin O.

\(d = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\)

\(\therefore\) the distance is 5.

(A distance is never negative, so \(-5\) is not admissible.)
